taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO; native from Oklahoma through Texas into northeastern and central Mexico.
look_here_first: Start with an erect COMPACT basal tuft of extremely thin, often inward-rolled blades, generally smaller than Lindheimer muhly. At bloom, confirm the delicate OPEN branching panicle, often reddish, with one-flowered awned spikelets. Inspect the membranous ligule and the small leaf width on a fresh blade under magnification; color alone is not diagnostic.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Purola Preserve documents M. reverchonii in the natural flora. Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed field treatment. Travis — USDA ARS herbarium specimen NA0074024 was collected along upper Bull Creek, about 7 mi NW of Austin.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Use exact specimen/local-flora evidence; do not infer counties solely from Edwards Plateau or Blackland Prairie ecoregion presence.

best_field_traits: densely tufted perennial bunchgrass with shallow condensed rhizome
very fine filiform/involute blades about 1–2 mm wide
membranous ligule usually around 2–4 mm, sometimes longer
panicle often develops reddish to pinkish-purple cast at bloom
spikelets larger/coarser than Lindheimer muhly, with lemmas roughly 3.5–5 mm
awn usually present and can extend several millimeters
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Muhlenbergia lindheimeri: Lindheimer muhly is much taller and coarser, with much longer ligules and a much larger feathery panicle. Muhlenbergia capillaris: Pink muhly can look similar at a glance but is not a project-native Central Texas taxon; use provenance plus blade/ligule/spikelet details rather than plume color. Muhlenbergia schreberi: Nimblewill has decumbent branching stems that root at lower nodes and forms low mats/patches rather than a compact basal tuft.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Whole flowering clump with panicle unobscured and ruler for height.
Close collar and true membranous ligule with mm ruler.
Fresh very narrow blade edge / involute cross-section.
Branching panicle and one awned one-flowered spikelet in macro.
Same-season same-scale compare with M. lindheimeri.
morphology_keys.crew_recognition_note: Start with an erect COMPACT basal tuft of extremely thin, often inward-rolled blades, generally smaller than Lindheimer muhly. At bloom, confirm the delicate OPEN branching panicle, often reddish, with one-flowered awned spikelets. Inspect the membranous ligule and the small leaf width on a fresh blade under magnification; color alone is not diagnostic.
morphology_keys.precision_caution: Some floras list seep-muhly ligules roughly 2–4 mm while a local Williamson County treatment gives many examples about 1–1.5 mm. Do not teach an absolute millimeter dividing line without specimen and variety context. The current local photos show fine basal blades but not diagnostic ligule, panicle or spikelet.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Lindheimer muhly has a much larger tougher bunch and comparatively contracted, densely flowered spikes plus generally longer ligules. Low creeping M. schreberi roots along nodes rather than forming a firm upright basal tuft. Nonlocal planted M. capillaris can have similar reddish-pink plumes; do not assume every pink ornamental is seep muhly.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Muhly field check — reverchonii
steps: Check for a tightly rooted upright tuft and very fine numerous leaves.
Find the delicate OPEN flowering panicle with small spikelets on slender branches; our two existing photos are dominated by foliage and this key flower part is MISSING.
Photograph the membranous ligule and isolated one-flowered spikelet with awn and a metric ruler; do not identify only by the pink haze.
